Study reliabilities in a meta-analysis

Source: vignettes/meta-analysis.Rmd
meta-analysis.Rmd

In a random-effects meta-analysis the studies play the part of the sites. A study’s reliability is the weight that its own estimate keeps in the empirical Bayes prediction of its true effect, and poolinfo’s diagnostics summarize these weights over the studies. In this vignette we fit a meta-analysis with metafor (Viechtbauer 2010) and compute the diagnostics in three ways: at metafor’s estimate of the between-study variance, over a confidence interval for it, and over its posterior. Along the way we relate them to the heterogeneity statistics that metafor prints. For the definitions of II, S‾\bar S, HH, VV and JeffJ_{\mathrm{eff}} (the informativeness, the mean reliability, the dispersion, the logit variance and the concentration count), see vignette("poolinfo").

library(poolinfo)
library(metafor)

metafor writes the between-study variance τ2\tau^2, and poolinfo writes it στ2\sigma_\tau^2 (sigma_tau^2 in its printed output). We use poolinfo’s notation from here on, so στ\sigma_\tau is the between-study standard deviation. poolinfo’s printed output calls the studies sites.

A meta-analysis of teacher expectancy effects

We use the data set dat.raudenbush1985 of the metadat package, which metafor loads. It has 19 studies of the effect of teachers’ expectations on their pupils’ IQ, each with a standardized mean difference and its sampling variance (Raudenbush 1984; Raudenbush and Bryk 1985). We fit the usual random-effects model by restricted maximum likelihood (REML).

dat <- dat.raudenbush1985
fit <- rma(yi, vi, data = dat, method = "REML")
fit
#> 
#> Random-Effects Model (k = 19; tau^2 estimator: REML)
#> 
#> tau^2 (estimated amount of total heterogeneity): 0.0188 (SE = 0.0155)
#> tau (square root of estimated tau^2 value):      0.1372
#> I^2 (total heterogeneity / total variability):   41.86%
#> H^2 (total variability / sampling variability):  1.72
#> 
#> Test for Heterogeneity:
#> Q(df = 18) = 35.8295, p-val = 0.0074
#> 
#> Model Results:
#> 
#> estimate      se    zval    pval    ci.lb   ci.ub    
#>   0.0837  0.0516  1.6208  0.1051  -0.0175  0.1849    
#> 
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

metafor estimates στ2\sigma_\tau^2 at 0.0188 and reports I2=41.9%I^2 = 41.9\% and H2=1.72H^2 = 1.72. As a proportion, its I2I^2 is σ̂τ2/(σ̂τ2+vtyp)\hat\sigma_\tau^2 / (\hat\sigma_\tau^2 + v_{\mathrm{typ}}), where vtypv_{\mathrm{typ}}, 0.0262 here, is the “typical” within-study variance of Higgins and Thompson (2002), which typical_variance() also computes. The familiar (Q−df)/Q(Q - \mathrm{df})/Q, here 0.50, agrees with it only when στ2\sigma_\tau^2 is estimated by the DerSimonian-Laird method (DerSimonian and Laird 1986), as the note in ?metafor::print.rma explains. metafor’s H2H^2 is 1/(1−I2)1/(1 - I^2), the ratio of the total variability to the sampling variability, and it has nothing to do with poolinfo’s dispersion HH.

The profile at the REML estimate

reliability_profile() takes the fit, computes the studies’ reliabilities at metafor’s estimate of στ\sigma_\tau, and summarizes them.

profile <- reliability_profile(fit)
profile
#> Reliability profile of 19 sites at sigma_tau = 0.137 (metafor REML estimate)
#> 
#>   informativeness I            0.351
#>   mean reliability             0.371
#>   dispersion H                 0.0748
#>   logit variance V             0.688
#>   concentration count J_eff    15.6 of 19
#> 
#> Site reliabilities range from 0.12 to 0.68.

At the REML estimate, II is 0.35, below metafor’s I2I^2 of 0.42, although both divide στ2\sigma_\tau^2 by στ2\sigma_\tau^2 plus a representative sampling variance. II uses the geometric mean of the sampling variances, 0.0348, which here is larger than the typical variance (with other variances it can be smaller). So II is the reliability of a study whose sampling variance is that geometric mean, and also what we get by averaging the studies’ reliabilities on the logit scale and transforming back (Lee 2026). Across the studies, the reliabilities range from 0.12 to 0.68. Each is the weight that a study’s own estimate keeps in its empirical Bayes prediction: blup(fit) returns μ̂+Sj(yj−μ̂)\hat\mu + S_j (y_j - \hat\mu) for study jj, with μ̂\hat\mu the estimated mean effect.

A profile at one value of στ\sigma_\tau carries no uncertainty about that value, and with 19 studies the uncertainty is large. metafor’s standard error of σ̂τ2\hat\sigma_\tau^2, 0.0155, is 82% of the estimate itself.

Confidence intervals mapped through the diagnostics

II and S‾\bar S increase with στ2\sigma_\tau^2, and so does JeffJ_{\mathrm{eff}} when the sampling variances differ, as they do here. A confidence interval for στ2\sigma_\tau^2 therefore maps to an interval for each of them with the same coverage. HH first rises and then falls, so its interval is the range of HH over the interval for στ2\sigma_\tau^2, which covers the true value at least as often. map_tau2_interval() maps the Q-profile interval of Viechtbauer (2007), which confint() also reports for this fit up to its default tolerance, and keeps it as an attribute.

mapped <- map_tau2_interval(fit)
mapped
#>   functional    estimate       lower       upper
#> 1          I  0.35138913  0.14432956  0.85050381
#> 2       mean  0.37148772  0.17259328  0.82160015
#> 3      J_eff 15.57711811 13.65786411 18.63387314
#> 4          H  0.07482955  0.04279031  0.08159594
attr(mapped, "interval")
#>    estimate       lower       upper 
#> 0.018826348 0.005861527 0.197700666

metafor’s confint() maps the same Q-profile interval through its own I2I^2:

confint(fit)
#> 
#>        estimate   ci.lb   ci.ub 
#> tau^2    0.0188  0.0059  0.1977 
#> tau      0.1372  0.0765  0.4447 
#> I^2(%)  41.8571 18.2934 88.3189 
#> H^2      1.7199  1.2239  8.5608

The Q-profile interval for στ2\sigma_\tau^2 runs from 0.0059 to 0.1977. Through II it becomes a 95% confidence interval from 0.14 to 0.85, and through metafor’s I2I^2 an interval from 18% to 88%. Both intervals have the coverage of the Q-profile interval and differ only in the representative sampling variance. Like everything else in poolinfo, they are conditional on the sampling variances.

The posterior and the restricted likelihood

reliability_posterior() takes the fit too. It computes the posterior of the diagnostics with flat priors on the mean and on στ\sigma_\tau, the package’s default, which vignette("posterior-summaries") discusses.

post <- reliability_posterior(fit)
post
#> Reliability profile of 19 sites (posterior)
#> Model: estimate ~ N(effect, se^2), effect ~ N(mean, sigma_tau^2),
#>        sites independent
#> Prior: flat on the mean and on sigma_tau
#> Summaries are conditional on the supplied standard errors.
#> Each site counts equally in the diagnostics, whatever its size.
#> 
#>                              mean     95% interval
#>   informativeness I          0.367    0.003    0.772
#>   mean reliability           0.374    0.004    0.743
#>   dispersion H               0.0602   0.0012   0.0816
#>   concentration count J_eff  15.4     11.9     18.3     of 19
#>   logit variance V           0.688    (fixed by the standard errors)
#>   sigma_tau                  0.151    0.0105   0.343
#>   effect mean                0.0866   -0.0212  0.218
#> 
#>   Pr(I > 0.5)                0.318
#>   I at E(sigma_tau^2)        0.467

With a posterior mean of 0.37 and a 95% posterior interval from 0.003 to 0.77, the posterior of II reaches values near 0, although the Q-profile interval for στ2\sigma_\tau^2 excludes 0. Each interval rests on a different statistic. With a flat prior on the mean, integrating the mean out of the likelihood leaves the restricted likelihood that REML maximizes (Harville 1974). Since the prior on στ\sigma_\tau is flat too, the posterior density of στ\sigma_\tau is proportional to that restricted likelihood. Its peak is at the REML estimate, σ̂τ=0.137\hat\sigma_\tau = 0.137, and at στ=0\sigma_\tau = 0 the density is still 0.53 of the peak. Cochran’s QQ, on which the Q-profile interval is built, is 35.8 at στ2=0\sigma_\tau^2 = 0, on 18 degrees of freedom (p=0.007p = 0.007).

A confidence interval built on the restricted likelihood behaves like the posterior. metafor’s profile likelihood interval, which ?metafor::confint.rma describes as more consistent with REML estimation, includes 0, and we map it through the diagnostics by giving map_tau2_interval() the sampling variances and the interval.

pl <- confint(fit, type = "PL")$random["tau^2", ]
mapped_pl <- map_tau2_interval(se2 = dat$vi, interval = c(
  estimate = fit$tau2, lower = pl[["ci.lb"]], upper = pl[["ci.ub"]]
))
mapped_pl
#>   functional    estimate    lower       upper
#> 1          I  0.35138913  0.00000  0.75161599
#> 2       mean  0.37148772  0.00000  0.72359190
#> 3      J_eff 15.57711811 11.81683 18.17332079
#> 4          H  0.07482955  0.00000  0.08159594

Mapped through II, the profile likelihood interval runs from 0.00 to 0.75, close to the posterior interval from 0.003 to 0.77, whereas the Q-profile interval gave 0.14 to 0.85.

A proper prior

With 19 studies we also want to know how much the flat prior on στ\sigma_\tau contributes. A half-normal prior with scale 0.5 is a reasonable proper alternative for standardized mean differences. It puts 95% of its mass below 0.98, so it allows true effects that vary from study to study by up to about one standard deviation of IQ and makes larger spreads unlikely. prior_sensitivity() refits the posterior under it and sets the two fits side by side.

prior_sensitivity(post, list(
  `half-normal, scale 0.5` = sd_prior("half_normal", scale = 0.5)
))
#> Comparison of 2 analyses
#> Intervals are central posterior intervals.
#> Each analysis is conditional on its own standard errors.
#> 
#>   analysis                J   informativeness I     mean reliability
#>   flat                    19  0.367 [0.003, 0.772]  0.374
#>   half-normal, scale 0.5  19  0.355 [0.003, 0.759]  0.363
#> 
#>   analysis                dispersion H             concentration count J_eff
#>   flat                    0.0602 [0.0012, 0.0816]  15.4
#>   half-normal, scale 0.5  0.0596 [0.0010, 0.0816]  15.3

With this prior, II has a posterior mean of 0.355 rather than 0.367, and its 95% posterior interval ends at 0.759 rather than 0.772. For these studies, then, our reading of the posterior is the same under either prior.

A moderator

With moderators, στ2\sigma_\tau^2 is the residual heterogeneity, the variance of the true effects around the meta-regression, and each study is pulled toward its own predicted value. Raudenbush (1984) related the effects to the weeks of contact between teachers and pupils before the expectations were induced. As in the example on the help page of dat.raudenbush1985, we cap the weeks at 3, so that the moderator distinguishes 0, 1, 2, and 3 or more weeks.

dat$weeks.c <- pmin(dat$weeks, 3)
fit_weeks <- rma(yi, vi, mods = ~ weeks.c, data = dat, method = "REML")
fit_weeks
#> 
#> Mixed-Effects Model (k = 19; tau^2 estimator: REML)
#> 
#> tau^2 (estimated amount of residual heterogeneity):     0.0000 (SE = 0.0072)
#> tau (square root of estimated tau^2 value):             0.0008
#> I^2 (residual heterogeneity / unaccounted variability): 0.00%
#> H^2 (unaccounted variability / sampling variability):   1.00
#> R^2 (amount of heterogeneity accounted for):            100.00%
#> 
#> Test for Residual Heterogeneity:
#> QE(df = 17) = 16.5708, p-val = 0.4838
#> 
#> Test of Moderators (coefficient 2):
#> QM(df = 1) = 19.2583, p-val < .0001
#> 
#> Model Results:
#> 
#>          estimate      se     zval    pval    ci.lb    ci.ub      
#> intrcpt    0.4072  0.0870   4.6782  <.0001   0.2366   0.5778  *** 
#> weeks.c   -0.1572  0.0358  -4.3884  <.0001  -0.2275  -0.0870  *** 
#> 
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

The REML estimate of the residual στ2\sigma_\tau^2 falls from 0.0188 to 0.0000, metafor’s R2R^2 is 100%, and the test for residual heterogeneity gives p=0.48p = 0.48. At that estimate the largest study reliability is 0.00007, so the profile at the REML estimate would pull every study all the way to its predicted value. Under the flat priors, the posterior instead weights each value of στ\sigma_\tau by its restricted likelihood, as we saw above, and we fit it for the meta-regression next.

post_weeks <- reliability_posterior(fit_weeks)
post_weeks
#> Reliability profile of 19 sites (posterior)
#> Model: estimate ~ N(effect, se^2), effect ~ N(x'beta, sigma_tau^2),
#>        sites independent
#> Prior: flat on the coefficients of the mean model and on sigma_tau
#> Summaries are conditional on the supplied standard errors.
#> Each site counts equally in the diagnostics, whatever its size.
#> 
#>                              mean     95% interval
#>   informativeness I          0.103    0.000    0.457
#>   mean reliability           0.117    0.000    0.464
#>   dispersion H               0.0263   0.0000   0.0800
#>   concentration count J_eff  13.0     11.8     16.4     of 19
#>   logit variance V           0.688    (fixed by the standard errors)
#>   sigma_tau                  0.0553   0.00202  0.171
#>   coefficient intrcpt        0.415    0.232    0.601
#>   coefficient weeks.c        -0.160   -0.238   -0.0845
#> 
#>   Pr(I > 0.5)                0.017
#>   I at E(sigma_tau^2)        0.129

With the moderator, the posterior mean of II falls from 0.37 to 0.10, with a 95% posterior interval from 0.00 to 0.46, and the posterior mean of στ\sigma_\tau from 0.151 to 0.055. Once the moderator accounts for most of the variation of the true effects, little of what remains can be told apart from sampling error. The model then pulls each study most of the way toward its predicted value. Now the flat prior is on the two coefficients of the meta-regression, and the printed output lists their posterior means and intervals.

The studies’ reliabilities

Here the sampling variances range from 0.0088 to 0.1391, a 16-fold range, and their logit variance is V=0.69V = 0.69. We plot the reliabilities of the model without the moderator, sorted, with their 95% posterior intervals.

plot_profile(post)

Study 4, by Pellegrini & Hicks, has the largest sampling variance and a posterior mean reliability of 0.16, and study 18, by Fleming & Anttonen, has the smallest variance and 0.61. Every study’s posterior interval starts below 0.02 and is at least 0.45 long, because the posterior of στ\sigma_\tau is wide, and the band of II runs from 0.003 to 0.77.

Your own meta-analysis

With your own meta-analysis, you pass the rma() fit to

  • reliability_profile() for the profile at its estimate,
  • map_tau2_interval() for confidence intervals, or
  • reliability_posterior() for the posterior, where its moderators become the mean model.

poolinfo reads fits of rma.uni(), the function behind rma(), which have one between-study variance and independent estimates. If your studies give several estimates each, you would model them with rma.mv(), whose fits poolinfo does not read. One option is then to combine the estimates of each study into one with metafor’s aggregate() method for escalc() data, under an assumed correlation within studies, and to fit rma() to the result.
